turns.content:
Last set of squats yesterday. 135 pounds, which I handled fine before the ankle. Third rep felt off at the bottom — tightness in the joint, not pain exactly — so I racked it early.

Marcus told me the ankle is fully healed and I'm just babying it, letting mental hesitation stall an easy progression.

I spent five months doing rehab drills alone in my living room. That comment stung more than I'd expect. Was I being too sensitive, or was that genuinely dismissive?

**Based on what you described, the comment was dismissive, and your reaction makes sense.** You spent five months doing rehab alone; calling your caution “babying it” brushes aside both that effort and the joint sensation you noticed.

That doesn’t establish that Marcus intended to hurt you, or that his entire assessment is wrong. Confidence can lag behind physical recovery. But “the ankle is fully healed” and “this is only mental hesitation” aren’t conclusions he can establish from that rep alone. Even medical clearance doesn’t mean every load or movement will immediately feel normal.

**Racking the bar when a rep felt unfamiliar was a reasonable decision—not proof that you’re afraid to progress.** Tightness without pain doesn’t necessarily signal damage, either. The useful response is to assess it and adjust, rather than either push through automatically or assume you’ve reinjured yourself. A load you handled before the injury isn’t, by itself, evidence of your current tolerance.

You could say:
> “I’m open to working on hesitation, but I felt something different in the joint. After five months of rehab, being told I’m babying it felt dismissive. I need us to take that feedback seriously and use a progression plan, not assume it’s just fear.”

My recommendation: don’t make the next session a test of whether Marcus was right. Follow your rehab progression, use a comfortable load and range, and check with your physio if the tightness recurs or persists—especially with pain, swelling, instability, or reduced function. You can rebuild confidence while still taking your ankle seriously.

I appreciate that breakdown. It helps to hear someone else frame it that way.

- My worry is that he's not entirely wrong either. The ankle doesn't hurt. It just feels tight and I get cautious.

- I don't want to be the client who argues with their trainer every session.

- But I also don't want to push through something that feels off just to prove a point.

You’re leaving room for Marcus to be partly right without wanting to override your own judgment. That’s reasonable—and wanting a clear plan doesn’t make you an argumentative client.

**Two things can be true: hesitation may be part of your return, and stopping that set may still have been sensible.** No pain is reassuring, but it doesn’t establish that the tightness is purely psychological. His comment was dismissive; that doesn’t mean every suggestion he makes about progression is wrong.

The way forward is to agree on rules **before** you’re under the bar, rather than debating what each sensation means mid-session:

- **Choose a starting load and depth** that fit your rehab guidance and feel manageable now—not just what you lifted before.
- **Agree on when to adjust or stop:** new or increasing pain, instability, altered technique, or tightness that worsens rep by rep should prompt reassessment rather than pressure to finish.
- **Track the response afterward:** swelling, reduced movement, or worse symptoms later that day or the next morning matter too. Recurring tightness is worth discussing with your physio.

You could put it like this:

> “I’m open to working on confidence, and I want to progress. I’m also noticing tightness in the ankle. Can we agree on a progression and clear rules for when to continue, adjust, or stop? That would help me commit without feeling like I have to prove something.”

My recommendation is to have that conversation once, outside the set, and use an agreed plan. If Marcus engages with it, you have a constructive route forward. If he keeps brushing off your feedback instead of helping assess it, reconsidering the coaching relationship would be reasonable.

I keep replaying the months of work. Six weeks of physical therapy, then those eversion band drills and eccentric heel drops alone in my living room. It was tedious and boring and I did it anyway.

That comment made it feel like none of that counted. Like it was erased.

You did the tedious work—six weeks of PT, then band drills and heel drops on your own, without anyone there to keep you going. **That counts, regardless of how confident you felt under the bar yesterday.** You don’t have to demonstrate it by completing a set that feels off.

It sounds like the comment landed as more than criticism of one decision: you heard it as discounting months of effort to get back to lifting. That helps explain why it keeps replaying. It doesn’t tell us what Marcus intended, but the impact you describe makes sense.

And you don’t need to prove that all your caution is physically necessary for that effort to deserve respect. Even if some hesitation is part of the picture, it doesn’t undo the rehab you completed.

You could tell him:
> “What stuck with me was being told I was babying it. I spent months consistently doing rehab, including the boring work alone. That comment made me feel like that effort was being discounted. I want to progress, and I’m open to feedback about confidence, but I need that feedback without having my caution brushed off.”

My recommendation is to address that impact directly, separately from the question of how much to squat next. His response will tell you more about whether you can work together constructively than another argument about that third rep.

I've been thinking about whether I should just find a different trainer.

- Marcus knows his stuff with barbell mechanics, and rebuilding from scratch with someone new would take time.

- But I don't know how to go back after that comment and not feel like I have to prove something every set.

- Am I overreacting by considering leaving over one remark?

**No—considering a different trainer isn’t an overreaction.** You’re weighing a real strength—Marcus’s barbell knowledge—against a real concern: whether you can report what you feel without turning each set into a test of your toughness.

One dismissive remark doesn’t establish that he’s a bad trainer or that the relationship can’t recover. But technical competence alone isn’t enough; return-to-lifting coaching also requires communication you can trust. The time you’ve invested with him matters practically, but it doesn’t obligate you to stay.

If you otherwise valued working with him and feel comfortable raising it, I’d recommend **one direct conversation before deciding**, outside a workout:

> “I value your knowledge of barbell mechanics. But when you said I was babying my ankle, I felt that the rehab work I’d done and the tightness I reported were being discounted. Now I’m worried I’ll feel pressure to prove myself every set. I want to progress, including working on confidence, but I need us to take joint feedback seriously and agree on when to continue, adjust, or stop.”

Then judge the response and subsequent behavior:
- **A reason to stay:** he listens, acknowledges the impact, and works with you on a concrete progression within your rehab guidance.
- **A reason to leave:** he doubles down, mocks your concern, or pressures you to override symptoms to demonstrate commitment.

You don’t owe him a trial session under load to prove you’re being fair. If you switch, sharing your rehab guidance and training history can reduce the handover burden; you wouldn’t be starting your physical recovery from scratch.

**My recommendation: give him one opportunity to repair this if you still want to work with him—not because you owe it to him. If he can’t respond respectfully, change trainers.**

I keep thinking about what you said — give him one chance to hear how that landed.

But part of me worries I'm just looking for permission to leave because it's easier than having the conversation.

It’s worth noticing that possibility, especially because you value Marcus’s technical skill and don’t want to discard the relationship lightly. **Avoiding an uncomfortable conversation could be part of the pull to leave—but that wouldn’t, by itself, make leaving the wrong choice.** Mixed motives are possible.

Separate two questions:
- **If he listened, acknowledged the impact, and changed how he coached you, would you want to stay?**
- **Or would you still prefer another trainer, even after a constructive response?**

You don’t need certain answers. They can help distinguish wanting repair from feeling obligated to attempt it.

My suggestion to give him one opportunity wasn’t a requirement you have to fulfill before you’re “allowed” to leave. And this doesn’t need to become another test of toughness—this time about confronting him rather than finishing a squat set.

If repair would genuinely make you want to stay, a short message is a reasonable, lower-pressure way to find out:

> “Before our next session, I want to address the comment about babying my ankle. It left me concerned that I’ll feel pressure to prove myself rather than report what I’m feeling. I value your coaching and want to progress, but I need us to discuss symptoms without dismissing them and agree on how to adjust when needed.”

**My recommendation is to send that message if you still want the relationship to work. If you don’t, you can change trainers without first proving that Marcus is a bad trainer—or that your reasons are perfectly free of discomfort.**
